body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: It would be unjust to this Theatre, in spite of Mr. Arnold's vagaries in the play-bills and in his own pieces, not to observe how well it continues to surpass its huge "classical" rival with respect to its new productions. Within a short period, a variety of wretched melo-dramas have wearied out the audiences at Covent-Garden; Mr. Reynolds has resorted to German trash which had already surfeited the public; and Mr. Dibdin, depending unluckily upon himself, has had a comedy damned—a final lesson, it is to be hoped, to that pertinacious retailer of Joe Miller. Within the same period at the Lyceum, we have had a comedy from a gentleman who has read Beaumont and Fletcher, an opera from Mr. Moore,—not worthy of him, it is true, but much superior to those of his contemporaries,—a play in imitation of the old English dramatists, and now we are presented with a farce by the author of the World and Raising the Wind. All this is highly creditable, and must be proportionately advantageous to the Managers; and even in revivals, they can make no vulgar stand by the side of Messrs. Harris and Kemble, if the matter is estimated by the real honour due to the pieces revived in the adequate performance of them; for though they have no pretensions to the revival of tragedies, yet the other theatre has as little to the revival of sterling comedies, in which women are concerned; and Dowton's single performance of the Hypocrite is a masterpiece of smooth and unaffected strength, which in point of acting may challenge all the revivals at Covent-Garden for the last ten years.

The new farce, called Turn Out, is founded on the inordinate self-opinion and irritability of Restive, an old politician, (Mr. Dowton), who is in possession of infallible schemes for liquidating the National Debt, and effecting a Coalition between England, North America, and the Cape of Good Hope; and is consequently eager to enjoy everybody's praises unalloyed with objection or doubt. By these humours he soon tires out his connexions, and gets into the hands of a hypocrite and parasite, Dr. Truckle (Lovegrove) who so works upon him by reading his manuscript and submitting to all his caprices, not excepting an occasional kick or two, that he turns his nephew (Phillips) out of doors, in order to make the Doctor sole heir to his wealth and master of his affections, and even sends for a distant female relative from Scotland in order to marry her to the old sinney. Unluckily however, the young lady, Marian Ramsey, (Miss Duncan) has long been in love with Somerville the nephew, though not aware hitherto of the relationship between them, and now discovering it, together with the artifices of Dr. Truckle, she alters her behaviour from pretending to be half an idiot to a course of seduction on the affections of the old gentleman, and in an interview with the Doctor, introductory to their proposed marriage, contrives not only to annoy him with an affectation of romance, but to alarm him against the match by hints of a previous connexion, of a nature sufficiently anticipating. His flat refusal of her, in consequence, irritates the uncle to such a degree, that he is turned out of doors after the nephew, and happening to meet with the latter, as he is going to sit down to dinner with his servant in the open air, is invited to join them with assurances of forgiveness and a promise of employment in the service of a widow, which together with the bumpers of wine poured down his throat by the valet operate so forcibly on his candour, that he drinks confusion to old politicians, and is in the midst of his reckless jollity, when the old gentleman, who has been brought that way on purpose, comes in upon his enjoyments, is received by him with snaps of his fingers, and of course receives his nephew with favour upon the spot. The hands of the lovers are then united, according to ancient "custom," and the truckling hypocrite, after being given to understand that the promise about the widow was all a jest, is carried off in drunkenness and despair.

The reader will discover in this story a resemblance to various incidents and characters already dramatized, particularly of Marian Ramsay and her tricks to Maria in the Citizen, and of Dr. Truckle to Dr. Cantwell in the Hypocrite. The idea of the politician was evidently suggested by a similar personage in the Lecture on Heads, who deals in caricature coalitions, talks of the Hottentots as being in the Protestant interest, and has a subtle scheme for bringing round his Catabaws from North America and making a diversion upon the settlements of the King of Tartary. Mr. Kenny's statesman, however, is as inferior to Stevens's in broad humour, as Marian Ramsay is to Maria; and Dr. Truckle has evidently no pretensions to a comparison with his original. Neither does the dialogue present anything particularly worthy of notice; it leaves nothing upon the recollection:—there is also a reprehensible coarseness in the insinuations that influence Truckle against the marriage, and the influence after all is misplaced in such a character, whose mercenary views are not at all likely to be delicate on the subject;—and to crown this list of imperfections, the words of the songs are almost as bad as Mr. Arnold himself could have written, and with the exception of one that is sung by Mr. Knight, are as badly set by Mr. King—but taken altogether, with its situations, its bustle of incident, and what it has copied from its betters, the farce, though unworthy of Mr. Kenney, is a very seeable one and improves in drollery as it proceeds. Miss Duncan’s performance gives a sort of half sketch of her Maria in the Citizen; Dowton, always masterly in his anger, which he can preserve from caricature even in its utmost violence, must of course give us some excellent touches in Restive;—Oxberry and Knight, two enamoured valets, have an amusing scene,—the most original indeed in the piece, in which they confide their secrets to each other, and produce the keepsakes which they received from their respective sweethearts;—and the conclusion is wound up with great effect by the impotent uproariousness of Lovegrove, and the flat profligacy under which he is caught out. Thus with the help of authors and actors, Mr. Kenney has succeeded in pleasing his audience, and in producing a farce that shall run for the season; but has the ambition of the author of the World sunk down to this? Does he please himself as well as a good-natured audience, and go to bed as content with it as they? It is to be hoped not; for though he no longer affords any reasonable expectation of being the restorer of the drama, and though it may appear ludicrous to others as well as himself to hear critics talking about his ambition, yet at least he should not grow worse and worse, and suffer his bad habits of writing to increase upon him, when fresh authors begin to look about them a little and to think for themselves.
